prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks

statement.case_for: After reading the other ballots I am moving my preferred configuration from B006 to B035. In my opening I ranked optical lattice clocks seventh, mainly because of overlap with earlier prizes for frequency combs and ion traps. Colleagues have shown that this worry is weaker than I made it. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a specific, original idea, and it was turned into clocks at the 1e-18 level that several independent laboratories now reproduce and compare. The clocks are already used to test constancy of fundamental constants and in relativistic geodesy, and the discussion of redefining the second gives timeliness. As someone who cares about gravity, I find a clock that resolves gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample a direct clue from nature of the kind I said we should look for. The attribution is also the cleanest of the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first strontium clocks, Ye for taking the performance and systematics to the frontier. That fits two laureates without the proxy-name problem I flagged for the Higgs collaborations.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and scope. The 2005 prize covered frequency combs, which Ye's group relies on, and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, which produced the first clocks beyond the microwave standard. A sceptical member can see lattice clocks as an excellent refinement of an already recognised toolkit and not a new discovery. Other clock groups (Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB and elsewhere, and the ion-clock community) are not credited, so a two-name prize will look incomplete to part of the community. It is also a precision-measurement achievement more than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and I still weigh the Higgs discovery higher in pure scientific significance.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B035 first as a clean idea (Katori's magic wavelength) and realization (Ye's systematics) that moved timekeeping to 1e-18, and notes that combs were recognised in 2005 but lattice clocks were not.
responses.response: I accept this and have moved up from my rank seven. Your point that the comb prize and the ion-clock prize addressed different steps persuades me. I would still keep the citation tied to the lattice-clock invention and its realization, not to a broad metrology programme, to answer your own uncertainty about whether Ye's credit is for clocks or for the wider comb and cold-matter work. I do not share your note that Wineland's earlier prize blurs the novelty. The trapping and interrogation of a large atom ensemble in a lattice is a different physical concept from a single-ion clock.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B008 first as a conceptually new class of matter, with the Z2 invariant and the HgTe experiment, and sees recognition as timely or overdue despite the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree B008 is a very strong case and I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is the credit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well route that Molenkamp measured, and the supplied names leave them out, so the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp triad does not fully describe the experimental discovery. Eriksson and Olsson raise the same point. I also see more overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize than you do. That is why I rank it behind the clocks, where the attribution is not contested in the same way.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery (B023) first as a landmark of instrument design, with a stable detector and a diffuse flux confirmed in several channels, but sees the division of credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering as uncertain.
responses.response: I share your admiration for a discovery of a new observational window, and it is the kind of case I normally favour. For this year I put it below the other candidates for two reasons you mention yourself: the origin of most of the flux is unresolved, and independent water-based confirmation is incomplete. A collaboration-scale prize with an arbitrary three-name selection is a weaker fit than a two-person lattice-clock prize. I would not object to B023 as a later prize once source identification is firmer.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B035 first and argues the timing is natural: combs in 2005, ion control in 2012, and now lattice clocks, with multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) confirming performance.
responses.response: Your multi-laboratory evidence is what changed my view on maturity. I disagree on one point. You treat the attribution as clean and I think we should be more careful. Lemonde's SYRTE group and the Sr and Yb groups did important parts of the work. The citation should say 'invention and realization' and not claim every clock result, so that the two-name prize reads as a fair statement of the decisive concept and its leading realization.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B004) first and distinguishes it from the macroscopic quantum tunnelling work honoured in 2025, while noting that Girvin and Huang are missing from the credit.
responses.response: I see the intrinsic merit, and the Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf structure is tidy. I still hesitate: Devoret was central to the 2025 prize and to circuit-QED developments, and a second superconducting-circuit prize within a year would be hard to defend to the wider community. You say you work in this field and may overvalue it, and I think that is a fair caution. I keep B004 behind the clocks for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges lattice clocks as a new invention or as incremental to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
Whether a two-name prize is fair to the other lattice-clock groups (for example SYRTE and the Sr and Yb groups) not credited here; I cannot verify priority details from the supplied text.
Whether the Higgs discovery (B006) would be better served by a collaboration-scale or leadership-based citation, which I cannot resolve from the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not appear among the credited names of the shortlisted candidates.
